overview: Fiji's history includes distinct iTaukei societies, Indo-Fijian communities and other peoples linked by settlement, trade and migration. Barkcloth, port buildings and labor records reveal skilled production and unequal colonial relationships. This card follows the colonial and independent country while identifying older traditions and later diaspora examples explicitly.

periods.title: British colonial government
periods.summary: Cession in 1874 established British colonial rule. Levuka was the first colonial capital, and imported indentured labor became central to the sugar economy. Independence followed in 1970.

periods.title: An independent Fiji
periods.summary: Fiji became independent on 10 October 1970. Its continuing national history includes distinct communities at home and cultural connections maintained by migrants overseas.

items.text: A painted masi cloth from the Lau Islands, dated to the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, survives at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Its stencilled designs provide a specific example of Fijian textile work; the collection record does not identify an excavated findspot.

Barkcloth makers softened strips of inner bark in water and beat them on a wooden anvil. Overlapping and beating the edges fused smaller pieces into larger sheets, turning plant fibers into flexible cloth without a loom.

A 1996 photograph records Mereia Johnston stencilling a border on paper-mulberry cloth in New Zealand. The named maker and workshop context show craft knowledge being practiced in the diaspora, rather than treating masi as only an anonymous museum survival.

At Levuka on Ovalau, warehouses and port buildings developed around the indigenous settlements of Totoga and Nasau. The surviving layout shows local communities shaping a colonial trading town, rather than an empty landscape simply filled by newcomers.

Beach Street's sea wall, lanes leading inland and traces of transport to the wharf connect buildings with movement of goods. Copra sheds, workers' cottages and the Baba labor settlement extend the story beyond official government buildings.
The colonial capital moved from Levuka to Suva in 1882, but commercial activity at Levuka continued. Losing capital status was a change in political function, not the abandonment of the town.

Indian indentured laborers first arrived in Fiji on 14 May 1879. Their contracts, remembered as girmit, tied them to harsh plantation labor. Their work and later community building are central to Fiji's history, while the coercion of the system must remain visible.

Yaqona, also called kava, is prepared from a plant root. It has ceremonial importance in iTaukei life and is also shared socially across communities. Its continued use overseas connects everyday gathering with relationships to Fiji.

Migration changed the circulation of food and household goods. Te Ara describes Indo-Fijian businesses in New Zealand helping make island and Indian ingredients, clothing and utensils more accessible to Fijian communities.

Fijian, Fiji Hindi and English connect different communities. Family use, contact with Fiji and language teaching help sustain them overseas, although language fluency and choices vary across generations.

Christian, Hindu and Muslim networks support worship, festivals and community relationships among migrants. These distinct institutions reveal the plurality of Fijian experience; no single religious practice represents the entire country.

Fiji became independent on 10 October 1970. The independence ceremony transferred political authority from colonial rule; it did not mark the beginning of the islands' peoples, craft traditions or community histories.

ending.text: British colonial rule ended with Fiji's independence in 1970. Fiji continues as a country whose communities maintain different histories, languages and traditions, including overseas. The colonial endpoint must not be turned into a claim that Fijian society ended.
